lesson.title: The Present Tense
lesson.subtitle: one stem, two endings, and the t that disappears in inversion

hook.title: One Stem, Two Endings
hook.content: Take the infinitive, remove -en, and you have the stem: werken → werk, maken → maak. Ik takes the bare stem; jij and hij add -t; wij, jullie and zij add -en.

pattern.title: The t moves with the pronoun
pattern.content: Jij werkt, but Werk jij? When jij follows the verb, the -t disappears. The t belongs to the subject-verb pair, not to the verb alone. This is the first place Dutch word order changes the shape of a word.
pattern.linguist_note: Dutch present-tense endings descend from older Germanic person markers; the inversion rule is a phonological repair, not a separate conjugation.
pattern.trap_note: Do not write werkt jij. In inversion, jij loses the -t: werk jij, kom jij, maak jij.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (The Present Tense):
exercises.target_answer: werken, maken, komen, gaan, jij, wij
exercises.meaning: to work, to make, to come, to go, you (informal singular), we
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "The Present Tense": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik werk hier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “The Present Tense”.

cues: The pattern: The t moves with the pronoun
exercises.explanation: “Jij werkt daar.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — The t moves with the pronoun.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not write werkt jij. In inversion, jij loses the -t: werk jij, kom jij, maak jij.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Wij komen samen.” is word-for-word “We come together.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: The t moves with the pronoun.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Hij maakt koffie.” reuses only material taught in “The Present Tense” — The t moves with the pronoun.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Hij maakt koffie.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising The t moves with the pronoun.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “Do you work tomorrow?”
twist.explanation: Inversion drops the -t on jij: werk jij, not werkt jij.

summary.outcome: Conjugate regular present-tense verbs and drop the -t after jij in inversion.
summary.takeaway: The stem is the launchpad; the endings follow the subject, and inversion changes the second-person shape.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Present Tense Drill.

werken.etymology_derivation: English work and Dutch werken are the same verb.

maken.etymology_derivation: English make and Dutch maken are the same verb; German shifted k to ch in machen.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

gaan.etymology_derivation: The same verb as English go, with the old g still pronounced.

jij.etymology_derivation: Dutch keeps the old singular thou as jij; English lost it outside dialect and poetry.

wij.etymology_derivation: The unstressed form is we; English we is the same pronoun.
